narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

Three factors weighed most heavily in this decision. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the single biggest reason the model expected you to struggle. Standing in only the second decile—well below the average of nearly sixth-decile among accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking in the second decile, also far below the typical sixth-decile level of admitted students, added further weight in the same direction. Finally, your LSAT score of 28 was noticeably lower than the average of 37 among those who were accepted, giving the model another clear signal that the exam would be difficult for you.

Taken together, these academic performance signals created a consistent picture that outweighed other information such as your solid 3.1 undergraduate GPA, middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a meaningfully higher score, while also improving your class rank in future coursework, would most directly improve your chances on a future application. Consider targeted bar-prep resources early so that, if admitted elsewhere, you enter with a plan to raise your first-time pass probability.
